title: Why synchronizing on String literal / interned object is a bug — use private final Object lock
shortTitle: Why is synchronizing on a String literal a bug?

s1_definition.profdef: Synchronizing on a String literal (`synchronized("LOCK")`) is a bug because String literals are **interned** — the JVM maintains a single instance per unique literal in the String pool. If TWO completely unrelated classes both synchronize on `"LOCK"`, they lock on the SAME object — causing unexpected blocking and potential deadlock between code that has nothing to do with each other. Same problem with `Boolean.TRUE`, `Integer.valueOf(1)` (cached -128 to 127), or any shared/interned object. Fix: ALWAYS use `private final Object lock = new Object()` — a dedicated lock object that ONLY your class knows about. Private: no external code can lock on it. Final: can't be reassigned to a different object. New Object: unique to your class.
s1_definition.analogy: Synchronizing on a String literal is like using the FRONT DOOR KEY of the building as your vault key. Every shop in the building has the same front door key. When you lock "your vault" with this key, you're actually locking the ENTIRE BUILDING — other shops can't enter. Two shops trying to lock at the same time → deadlock. Fix: each shop gets its OWN unique key (private final Object) that nobody else has.
s1_definition.oneliner: String literals are interned → SHARED across entire JVM. synchronized("LOCK") = global lock affecting ALL code using "LOCK". Fix: private final Object lock = new Object() — unique, private, not shared.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Synchronizing on a String literal (`synchronized("LOCK")`) is a bug because String literals are **interned** — the JVM maintains a single instance per unique literal in the String pool. If TWO completely unrelated classes both synchronize on `"LOCK"`, they lock on the SAME object — causing unexpected blocking and potential deadlock between code that has nothing to do with each other. Same problem with `Boolean.TRUE`, `Integer.valueOf(1)` (cached -128 to 127), or any shared/interned object. Fix: ALWAYS use `private final Object lock = new Object()` — a dedicated lock object that ONLY your class knows about. Private: no external code can lock on it. Final: can't be reassigned to a different object. New Object: unique to your class.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Synchronizing on a String literal is like using the FRONT DOOR KEY of the building as your vault key. Every shop in the building has the same front door key. When you lock "your vault" with this key, you're actually locking the ENTIRE BUILDING — other shops can't enter. Two shops trying to lock at the same time → deadlock. Fix: each shop gets its OWN unique key (private final Object) that nobody else has.

**One line to remember:** String literals are interned → SHARED across entire JVM. synchronized("LOCK") = global lock affecting ALL code using "LOCK". Fix: private final Object lock = new Object() — unique, private, not shared.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — Two unrelated microservices (AccountService and AuditService) in the same JVM both used `synchronized("GLOBAL")`.** The AuditService held the lock for 10 seconds during report generation. During those 10 seconds, AccountService debits were BLOCKED — customers couldn't withdraw money. The services had no intentional relationship — the shared String literal was a coincidence. Fix: each service gets its own `private final Object lock = new Object()`. No accidental sharing.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Service-A enters `synchronized("SHARED_LOCK")` → acquires the interned String's monitor lock.

**Step 2.** Service-B (unrelated code) enters `synchronized("SHARED_LOCK")` → SAME interned String object → BLOCKED! Waits for Service-A.

**Step 3.** Service-A finishes after 500ms → releases lock → Service-B unblocked → enters. Total delay: 500ms for completely unrelated code!

**Step 4.** Fix: each service uses `private final Object lock = new Object()`. Service-A's lock and Service-B's lock are different objects → never block each other → parallel.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ BUG: String literal lock (shared!) ═══

  AccountService: synchronized("LOCK") → lock on interned "LOCK"
  AuditService:   synchronized("LOCK") → SAME object → BLOCKED!
  "LOCK" == "LOCK" → true! (interned String pool)

  ═══ FIX: private final Object (unique!) ═══

  AccountService: private final Object lock1 = new Object();
  AuditService:   private final Object lock2 = new Object();
  lock1 != lock2 → different objects → PARALLEL!

  ═══ DANGEROUS SHARED OBJECTS ═══
  "any string literal"    → interned, shared across JVM
  Boolean.TRUE/FALSE      → cached, shared
  Integer.valueOf(-128..127) → cached, shared
  this                    → accessible to external code
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Lock Isolation Between Services ═══

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  JVM (Single Process)                             │
  │                                                    │
  │  ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐        │
  │  │ AccountService  │  │ AuditService    │        │
  │  │ lock: private   │  │ lock: private   │        │
  │  │ final Object    │  │ final Object    │        │
  │  │ (unique!)       │  │ (unique!)       │        │
  │  └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘        │
  │  ← Different locks → run in PARALLEL              │
  │                                                    │
  │  (Avoid) If both used synchronized("LOCK"):            │
  │  ← SAME interned string → BLOCK each other!      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — String Pool + Lock Object ═══

  JVM String Pool:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  "LOCK" → one instance at address 0xABC │
  │  "HELLO" → one instance at address 0xDEF│
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  AccountService: synchronized("LOCK") → lock on 0xABC
  AuditService:   synchronized("LOCK") → lock on 0xABC (SAME!)
  → Unrelated services block each other!

  ═══ CORRECT DESIGN ═══

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │  AccountService               │
  │  - lock: private final Object│  address: 0x111 (unique!)
  │  + debit(): synchronized(lock)│
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │  AuditService                 │
  │  - lock: private final Object│  address: 0x222 (unique!)
  │  + report(): synchronized(lock)│
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  0x111 ≠ 0x222 → different monitors → no blocking!
  Rules: PRIVATE (no external access) + FINAL (no reassign) + new Object (unique)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Synchronizing on a String literal is a bug because String literals are interned — the JVM stores one instance per unique literal in the String pool. If two completely unrelated classes synchronize on `"LOCK"`, they lock on the SAME object, causing unexpected blocking and potential deadlock. The same applies to `Boolean.TRUE`, `Integer.valueOf()` in the cached range (-128 to 127), and any other shared/pooled object.

The fix is `private final Object lock = new Object()`. PRIVATE: no external code can access your lock → no accidental contention from other classes. FINAL: the lock reference can't be reassigned → you always synchronize on the same object (reassigning would silently break synchronization). new Object(): creates a unique instance → not shared with anyone. Also avoid `synchronized(this)` — external code holding a reference to your object can lock on it, causing unexpected blocking. In banking: AccountService and AuditService both used `synchronized("GLOBAL")` → audit report generation blocked all account operations for 10 seconds. Fix: separate private locks.

---

keyPoints: String literals are interned — same literal across classes is SAME object
Unrelated classes syncing on same string block each other
Fix: private final Object lock = new Object()
